opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it didn't feel like a sudden decision from the inside. It felt more like a convergence of things I'd been thinking about for years.

I've loved mathematics since I was quite young. Competitions, then research, and the whole time I was thinking about what it actually means to *do* math: to have an intuition, turn it into a conjecture, and then build a proof that's airtight. Over the last few years, watching what large models could do, I kept asking whether the reasoning I cared about could be partly automated, or at least dramatically amplified. That question didn't come from reading headlines. It came from sitting with hard problems and knowing how much of the process was search, verification, and bookkeeping that a machine could help with.

So when I asked myself whether this was a trend, I tried to separate two things. One is "AI is hot, so I should do an AI company." The other is "there's a specific problem I understand deeply, the technology has just reached the point where it's tractable, and I'm in a rare position to work on it." The first is impulsive. The second is a judgment about timing. With formal verification tools like Lean maturing, and models getting better at reasoning, the window felt real, and it felt like it wouldn't stay open forever.

I also tested myself. If AI fell out of fashion tomorrow, would I still want to work on this? The answer was yes. I'd still want to build systems that can discover and verify mathematics. That told me the motivation was intrinsic, not borrowed from the hype cycle.

And practically, I talked to a lot of people: mathematicians, researchers, people who had built companies. I let them poke holes in the idea. When the idea survived that and I still couldn't stop thinking about it, I knew it wasn't a whim. It was something I'd regret not trying.

r001.rationale: The response says her decision grew from longstanding interest in mathematics and a specific opportunity in AI, but it does not identify prior strong opposition to becoming an AI founder as her reason for ruling out trend-following.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the confidence came less from a single moment of decision and more from the fact that there was never really a moment of decision at all. If I look back, the path to founding Axiom was something I'd been walking for a long time before I ever called it a company.

I grew up doing math. Competition math, then research math at MIT, then Oxford and Stanford. And the thing that always bothered me, even as a teenager, was how much of mathematical progress depended on a very small number of people having a very specific kind of intuition at a very specific moment. Proofs would sit unverified for years. Ideas would get rediscovered because nobody could search the literature properly. It felt like the most rigorous discipline humans have ever built was being run on extremely fragile infrastructure.

So when language models started getting good enough to reason in formal systems, I didn't experience that as "oh, AI is hot, I should jump in." I experienced it as "the thing I've been frustrated by for ten years might finally be solvable." The problem came first. The technology arrived second. That ordering matters a lot to me, because I think most impulsive founders have it reversed. They see a wave, and then they go looking for a problem to justify riding it.

The other reason I was confident is that I'd already tested myself against the alternative. I was on a very comfortable academic track. I'd had the fellowships, the offers, the clear sense of what the next decade would look like if I stayed. And I kept finding that I didn't want it. Not because academia is bad, but because I could see the ceiling. The question I cared about, whether we can build systems that genuinely do mathematics rather than imitate it, is not a question you can answer by writing papers alone. You need to build the thing, at scale, with engineers and compute and users who will tell you when you're wrong.

And there's a simpler test, too. If the AI hype disappeared tomorrow, if the funding dried up and the headlines moved on, would I still want to do this? The answer was yes without hesitation. I'd do it slower, with fewer resources, but I'd do it. When the answer to that question is yes, I think you can stop worrying about whether you're following a trend. You're just doing the work you were always going to do, and the trend happens to be blowing in the same direction for now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says her path to founding Axiom had been underway for a long time and that the problem preceded the technology. It does not identify prior strong opposition to becoming an AI founder as the reason she ruled out trend-following.

astra-6.text:
For me, the confidence came from separating two questions: am I excited about AI, and do I actually want the work of building a company? Those aren’t the same thing. You can be fascinated by the technology without wanting to spend your days recruiting, talking to users, making difficult decisions, and dealing with uncertainty.

I didn’t need to be certain that a company would succeed. I needed to believe that the problems were worth working on and that I wanted the responsibility of trying to solve them. The question I kept coming back to was: if AI stopped being fashionable, would I still want to do this? That was a much more useful test than how excited I felt in any particular moment.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes enthusiasm for AI from wanting to build a company and asks whether she would continue if AI stopped being fashionable. It does not identify Carina Hong’s prior strong opposition to becoming an AI founder as her reason.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the distinction was whether I was excited about being a founder or about the work itself. If you take away the attention around AI and the title of founder, do I still want to spend my time working on these problems? Would I still choose this if progress were slow and nobody was paying attention?

That was how I thought about it. Confidence didn’t mean knowing that a company would succeed. It meant feeling that the underlying motivation was durable—that I wanted to do the work, including the difficult and unglamorous parts, rather than simply participate in a trend.

r001.rationale: The response describes durable interest in the work as evidence against trend-following, but does not identify Carina Hong’s prior strong opposition to becoming an AI founder.
